'''Alex Szalay''' is a [[Bloomberg Distinguished Professorships|Bloomberg Distinguished Professor]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Bloomberg Distinguished Professorships|url= http://web.jhu.edu/administration/provost/BDP}}</ref> of physics and astronomy<ref>{{cite web|title= Alexander Szalay Faculty Page|date= 8 February 2013|url= http://physics-astronomy.jhu.edu/directory/alexander-s-szalay/}}</ref> and computer science<ref>{{cite web|title= Alexander Szalay Faculty Page, Department of Computer Science|url= https://www.cs.jhu.edu/faculty/alex-szalay/?repeat=w3tc}}</ref> at the [[Johns Hopkins University School of Arts and Sciences]] and [[Whiting School of Engineering]].<ref name="hub.jhu.edu">Brooks, Kelly [https://hub.jhu.edu/2015/03/30/bloomberg-professors-casadevall-chute-salzberg-szalay "Johns Hopkins names four new Bloomberg Distinguished Professors"], ''JHU Hub'', Baltimore, 30 March 2015. Retrieved on 27 July 2015.</ref> Szalay is an international leader in [[astronomy]], [[cosmology]], the science of [[big data]], and [[data-intensive computing]]. In 2023, he was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2023-nas-election.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230502194908/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2023-nas-election.html | url-status=dead | archive-date=May 2, 2023 | title=2023 NAS Election }}</ref>

==Biography==
Alexander Sándor Szalay, Jr. was born in Hungary. His father is [[Sándor Szalay (physicist)|Sándor Szalay]], who is considered “the father of nuclear physics in Hungary” for his discovery of a natural [[Enriched uranium|enrichment mechanism of uranium]] and [[neutrino]]s.<ref name="Simon 1998 213">{{cite book|last= Simon|first= Andrew|date= 1998|title= Made in Hungary: Hungarian Contributions to Universal Culture|url= https://archive.org/details/madeinhungaryhun0000simo/page/213|location= USA|publisher= Simon Publications LLC|page= [https://archive.org/details/madeinhungaryhun0000simo/page/213 213]|isbn= 978-0966573428|access-date= 27 July 2015|url-access= registration}}</ref>  Szalay graduated with a Bachelor of Science degree in [[Physics]] in 1969 from Kossuth University, now [[University of Debrecen]], in Hungary. He then received a Master of Science in [[Theoretical Physics]] 1972 and a [[Doctorate|Ph.D]] in [[Astrophysics]] in 1975 from the [[Eötvös Loránd University]] in Budapest.<ref>{{cite web|title=Alexander Sandor Szalay CV |url= http://krieger.jhu.edu/physics/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2013/02/Szalay.pdf}}</ref> During this period, from 1974 to 1982, Szalay also played guitar in the Hungarian rock band [[Panta Rhei (band)]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sdss.jhu.edu/~szalay/music/pantarhei.html|title=Panta Rhei|access-date=29 July 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150801161342/http://www.sdss.jhu.edu/%7Eszalay/music/pantarhei.html|archive-date=2015-08-01|url-status=dead}}</ref> After graduation Szalay spent postdoctoral periods at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], [[University of Chicago]], and [[Fermilab]], before accepting an assistant professorship at [[Eötvös Loránd University]] in 1982. After rising to the rank of full professor at Eötvös, he joined [[Johns Hopkins University]] in 1989. Subsequently, he was named the Alumni Centennial Chair in 1998 and earned a secondary appointment in the Department of Computer Science in 2001. In 2008, he became Doctor Honoris Causa of the [[Eötvös Loránd University]].

In March 2015, Szalay was named a [[Bloomberg Distinguished Professorships|Bloomberg Distinguished Professor]] at [[Johns Hopkins University]] for his accomplishments as an interdisciplinary researcher and excellence in teaching.<ref>{{cite web|title=Michael R. Bloomberg commits $350 million to Johns Hopkins for transformational academic initiative|url= https://hub.jhu.edu/2013/01/26/bloomberg-gift|date= 2013-01-26}}</ref><ref name=anderson>Anderson, Nick. [https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/education/bloomberg-pledges-350-million-to-johns-hopkins-university/2013/01/26/9c0e1a5a-67d6-11e2-93e1-475791032daf_story.html "Bloomberg pledges $350 million to Johns Hopkins University"], ''The Washington Post'', Washington, D.C., 23 January 2013. Retrieved on 12 March 2015.</ref> The Bloomberg Distinguished Professorship program was established in 2013 by a gift from [[Michael Bloomberg]].<ref>Barbaro, Michael. [https://www.nytimes.com/2013/01/27/nyregion/at-1-1-billion-bloomberg-is-top-university-donor-in-us.html?_r=0 "$1.1 Billion in Thanks From Bloomberg to Johns Hopkins"], ''[[The New York Times]]'', New York, 26 January 2013. Retrieved on 1 March 2015.</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Michael R. Bloomberg Commits $350 Million to Johns Hopkins for Transformational Academic Initiative 2013|url= http://releases.jhu.edu/2013/01/26/michael-r-bloomberg-commits-350-million-to-johns-hopkins/}}</ref> Szalay holds joint appointments in the [[Johns Hopkins University]] [[Zanvyl Krieger School of Arts and Sciences]]’s Department of Physics and Astronomy<ref>{{cite web|title= Alexander S. Szalay|date= 8 February 2013|url= http://physics-astronomy.jhu.edu/directory/alexander-s-szalay/}}</ref> and the [[Whiting School of Engineering]]’s Department of [[Computer Science]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Johns Hopkins Department of Computer Science - Alex Szalay|url= https://www.cs.jhu.edu/faculty/alex-szalay/?repeat=w3tc}}</ref> Through the [[Bloomberg Distinguished Professorships|Bloomberg Distinguished Professorship]], Szalay also will be teaching a new undergraduate class in data science, using a synthesis of statistics, computer science, and basic sciences that he thinks “will become the fundamental language used by the next generation of scientists.”<ref name="hub.jhu.edu"/>

Since 2009, Szalay has been the founding director of the Institute for Data Intensive Engineering and Science (IDIES) at Johns Hopkins, an interdisciplinary institute fostering “education and research in applying [[Data-intensive computing|data-intensive]] technologies to problems of national interest in physical and biological sciences and engineering.” At the time of its founding, IDIES was the “first interdisciplinary [[big data]] center of its type […] and has since inspired similar efforts at other universities.”<ref name="Johns Hopkins University">{{cite web |url= http://krieger2.jhu.edu/pubs/physics/2013/features.html|title= The Next Scientific Revolution: Big Data|last1=Popkin |first1= Gabriel|date= Summer 2013 |publisher= Johns Hopkins University|access-date= 28 July 2015 }}</ref> IDIES is supported by the [[National Science Foundation]], [[NASA]], [[Intel]], [[Microsoft]], [[Nokia]], [[Nvidia]], the [[Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation]], and the [[W. M. Keck Foundation]].<ref>{{cite web|title=IDIES|url= https://idies.jhu.edu/}}</ref>

=== Awards and distinctions ===
In 1990, Szalay was elected to the [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]] as a Corresponding Member and awarded the E.W. Fullam Prize of the Dudley Observatory.<ref>{{cite web |title=CIFAR Program Members - Alexander S. Szalay |url=http://www.cifar.ca/alexander-s-szalay |access-date=2015-07-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151001104939/http://www.cifar.ca/alexander-s-szalay |archive-date=2015-10-01 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The following year, he received Hungary's [[Széchenyi Prize]], which recognizes “those who have made an outstanding contribution to academic life in Hungary.”<ref>{{cite web|title= Széchenyi Prizes of 2014|url=https://dailynewshungary.com/szechenyi-prizes-of-2014/|date=2014-03-20}}</ref> Szalay was recognized in particular for his “discovery of the large scale (400 million light years) distribution pattern of galaxies.”<ref name="Simon 1998 213"/> In 2003, he was elected as a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]. In 2004, he received an [[Humboldt Prize|Alexander Von Humboldt Research Award]] in Physical Sciences. In 2007, Szalay received the [[Jim Gray (computer scientist)#Jim Gray eScience Award|Jim Gray eScience Award]] in recognition for his “foundational contributions to interdisciplinary advances in the field of astronomy and groundbreaking work with [[Jim Gray (computer scientist)|Jim Gray]].”<ref>{{cite web|title=Jim Gray eScience Award|url= http://research.microsoft.com/en-us/collaboration/focus/escience/jim-gray-award.aspx}}</ref> The [[IEEE Computer Society]] awarded Szalay with the 2015 [[Sidney Fernbach Award]] for "his outstanding contributions to the development of data-intensive computing systems and on the application of such systems in many scientific areas including astrophysics, turbulence, and genomics.”.<ref>{{cite web|title=2015 Sidney Fernbach Award Recipient|url=http://www.computer.org/web/awards/fernbach-alexander-szalay|access-date=2015-09-30}}</ref> In 2023 he has been elected to the National Academy of Sciences. In 2024, he became a Fellow of the ACM.

==Research==
Szalay is an astrophysicist who has made significant contribution to our understanding of the [[structure formation]] and on the nature of the [[dark matter]] in the [[universe]]. Distinguished in the area of the [[cosmology]], he works on the [[statistical]] measures of the spatial distribution of [[Galaxy|galaxies]] and [[Galaxy formation and evolution|galaxy formation]]. He has contributed much to the field of [[theoretical astrophysics]] and [[Observable universe#Large-scale structure|large scale structure]]. Szalay has developed several novel statistical techniques about optimal estimators for galaxy correlations, [[Spectral density#Power spectral density|power spectra]], [[photometric redshift]]s for galaxies, optimal co-adding of multicolor images, PCA-based [[spectral classification]] of galaxies and [[Bayesian probability|Bayesian]] techniques applied to spatial cross-matching of different [[astronomical catalogs]]. He has also led the development of [[Data-intensive computing|data-intensive]] [[computer architecture]]s covering all aspects of this process from design to implementation.

Particular accomplishments include:
* Biased [[Galaxy formation and evolution|galaxy formation]] in a [[cold dark matter]] dominated universe
* Structure formation in a [[neutrino]]-dominated universe
* Computing the power spectrum in hot, cold and warm [[dark matter]] dominated universes (Szalay also defined the terms hot/cold/warm dark matter)
* Various measurements of the large scale [[galaxy]] [[Spectral density#Power spectral density|power spectrum]]

=== Sloan Digital Sky Survey ===
Professor Szalay is the Architect for the Science Archive and Chair of the Science Council of the [[Sloan Digital Sky Survey]], the most used astronomy facility in the world today.<ref>{{cite journal|last1= Szalay |first1= Alexander|last2=Gray |first2= Jim |title= The Sloan Digital Sky Survey and its Archive |arxiv=astro-ph/9912382 |journal= ASP Conference Series |volume=216 |year=2000 |pages= 1–10 |bibcode = 2000ASPC..216..405S }}</ref> He collaborated with [[Jim Gray (computer scientist)|Jim Gray]] to design an efficient system to perform [[data mining]] on the SDSS [[Terabyte]] sized archive, based on innovative [[Spatial database|spatial indexing]] techniques, that represented a “thousand-fold increase in the total amount of data that astronomers have collected to date.”<ref>{{cite web|url= https://skyserver.sdss.org/dr9/en/skyserver/cise/|title= Special Issue of Computing in Science and Engineering Dedicated to the SDSS Science Archive |access-date=28 July 2015}}</ref> The SDSS Science Archive has attracted an unprecedented number of users, and is considered to be an example for online archives of the future. Currently, he is on the Science Advisory Council of the [[Large Synoptic Survey Telescope]].

A [[minor planet]] discovered by the [[Sloan Digital Sky Survey]] at [[Apache Point Observatory]] was named [[Meanings of minor planet names: 170001–171000|170010 Szalay]] in his honor.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/sbdb.cgi?sstr=170010|title=170010 Szalay (2002 TJ341)|access-date=28 July 2015}}</ref>

=== Virtual observatory and cosmological simulations ===
Szalay is a leader in the grass-roots standardization effort to bring the next generation [[Petascale computing|petascale]] databases in astronomy to a common basis, so that they will be interoperable. In support of this goal, Szalay was Project Director of the [[National Virtual Observatory]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://virtualobservatory.org/whatis/history.aspx|title=History of the Virtual Astronomical Observatory|access-date=28 July 2015}}</ref> In 2001, [[Jim Gray (computer scientist)|Jim Gray]] and Szalay wrote up a viewpoint article on the national virtual observatory project for ''Science'', entitled "The World-Wide Telescope."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Szalay |first1= Alexander|last2= Gray|first2=Jim |date= 14 September 2001|title= The World-Wide Telescope|url= http://virtualobservatory.org/documents/wwt.pdf|journal=Science|publisher= [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]|volume= 293|issue= 5537|pages= 2037–2040|doi= 10.1126/science.293.5537.2037|pmid= 11557879|access-date=27 July 2015|bibcode = 2001Sci...293.2037S }}</ref> He was also one of the founders of the [[International Virtual Observatory Alliance]] and part of the core team to build the [[Galaxy Zoo]],<ref>{{cite journal| display-authors=8| author=C.J. Lintott| author2=K. Schawinski| author3=A. Slosar| author4=K. Land| author5=S. Bamford| author6=D. Thomas| author7=M. Jordan Raddick| author8=R.C. Nichol| author9=A.Szalay| author10=D. Andreescu| author11=P. Murray| author12=J. van den Berg| date=2008| title=Galaxy Zoo: morphologies derived from visual inspection of galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey| journal=[[MNRAS]]| volume=389| issue=3| bibcode=2008MNRAS.389.1179L| doi=10.1111/j.1365-2966.2008.13689.x| arxiv=0804.4483| pages=1179–1189| doi-access=free| s2cid=15279243}}</ref><ref>{{ cite journal|title=Galaxy Zoo 1: data release of morphological classifications for nearly 900,000 galaxies| display-authors=8| author=C. Lintott| author2=K. Schawinski| author3=S. Bamford| author4=A. Slosar| author5=K. Land| author6=D. Thomas| author7=E. Edmondson| author8=K. Masters| author9=R. Nichol| author10=J. Raddick| author11=A. Szalay| author12=D. Andreescu| author13=P. Murray| author14=J. Vandenberg| date=2011| journal=[[MNRAS]]|volume=410| issue=1| bibcode=2011MNRAS.410..166L| doi=10.1111/j.1365-2966.2010.17432.x| arxiv=1007.3265| pages=166–178| doi-access=free| s2cid=56460191}}</ref> one of the most visible citizen science projects today.

Szalay collaborated with [[Simon White]] and Gerard Lemson to build a database similar to the [[Sloan Digital Sky Survey#Data access|SkyServer]] out of the [[Millennium Run|Millennium Simulation]], which became the reference cosmology simulation used by astronomers all over the world.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.atnf.csiro.au/research/workshops/2013/astroinformatics/talks/szalay-sydney-2013.pdf|title= From SDSS to Simulations: Data Intensive Astrophysics|access-date=28 July 2015}}</ref> In collaboration with Piero Madau, he is building the 1.2PB database, known as The Milky Way Laboratory, for the Silver River cosmology simulation, currently running at [[Oak Ridge National Laboratory]].<ref>{{cite web|url= https://indico.cern.ch/event/116485/session/1/contribution/5/attachments/53752/77316/szalay-fnal-2011.pdf|title= Presentation at CERN: Data Analysis and Access in Astrophysics|access-date=28 July 2015}}</ref>

=== Data-intensive computing ===
Szalay was involved in the early projects related to the [[Grid computing|Computational Grid]], in particular the GriPhyN and iVDGL projects, creating [[testbed]] [[application software|applications]] for [[Particle physics|high energy physics]] and [[astrophysics]]. He has collaborated on high-speed [[data analysis|data analytics]] for more than a decade, and has been part of the TeraFlow project<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.glif.is/apps/teraflow.html |title= Teraflow Testbed: High Performance Flows for Large Distributed Data Archives |access-date=28 July 2015}}</ref> since 2004 <ref>{{cite journal|url= http://grantome.com/grant/NSF/ACI-0430781 |title= SCI: II: The TeraFlow Project: High Performance Flows for Mining Large Distributed Data Archives |journal= Grantome |access-date=28 July 2015|last1= Szalay |first1= Alexander |last2= Grossman |first2= Robert }}</ref> and the Open Science Grid.<ref>{{cite journal|url= http://grantome.com/grant/NSF/ACI-1137045 |title= 100G Connectivity for Data-Intensive Computing at JHU |journal= Grantome |access-date=28 July 2015|last1= Zarriello |first1= Dean |last2= Terzis |first2= Andreas |last3= Bagger |first3= Jonathan |last4= Robbins |first4= Mark |last5= Szalay |first5= Alexander }}</ref> He was also heavily involved in the Data Conservancy, researching the long-term curation and preservation of [[scientific data]].<ref>{{cite web|url= https://dataconservancy.org/community/partners/|title= The Data Conservancy's partners provide the building blocks for addressing data curation needs.|access-date= 28 July 2015|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20150813004733/http://dataconservancy.org/community/partners/|archive-date= 13 August 2015|url-status= dead|df= dmy-all}}</ref>

He has coauthored several papers with [[Gordon Bell]], one of the world's premier computer designers, arguing how [[Amdahl's law]] can be used to revisit [[data-intensive computing]] architectures from first principles.<ref>{{cite book |last1= Szalay|first1= Alexander|last2= Bell|first2= Gordon|title= 2009 42nd Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences|chapter= GrayWulf: Scalable Clustered Architecture for Data Intensive Computing|date= 5 January 2009|publisher= IEEE|pages= 1–10|doi= 10.1109/HICSS.2009.234|isbn= 978-0-7695-3450-3|s2cid= 7837424}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1= Szalay|first1= Alexander|last2= Bell|first2= Gordon|date= 12 March 2010|title= Low-power amdahl-balanced blades for data intensive computing|journal= ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review|publisher= ACM|volume= 44|issue= 1|pages= 71–75|doi= 10.1145/1740390.1740407|citeseerx= 10.1.1.495.8904|s2cid= 2511908}}</ref> Applying these ideas, he built a low power system, GrayWulf, using Atom processors with extremely good IO performance per unit power (factor of 15 better than a typical rack server).<ref>{{cite web |url= http://research.microsoft.com/en-us/collaboration/focus/e3/graywulf.aspx|title= GrayWulf Takes Byte Out of Data Overload|date= 2009 |publisher= [[Microsoft]]|access-date= 28 July 2015 }}</ref> GrayWulf was named in homage to and builds on the work of Szalay's collaborator legendary Microsoft computer scientist [[Jim Gray (computer scientist)|Jim Gray]] and Beowulf, the “original computer cluster developed at [[NASA]] using ‘off-the-shelf’ computer hardware.”<ref name="Johns Hopkins University"/> Szalay led the team that won the Supercomputing Data Challenge in SC-08 - the International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis - with their entry "Storage Challenge GrayWulf: Scalable Clustered Architecture for Data-Intensive Computing."<ref>{{cite web|url= http://sc08.supercomputing.org/html/AwardsPresented.html|title= SC Challenge Awards|access-date= 27 July 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url= http://sc08.supercomputing.org/scyourway/conference/view/storc104.html|title= SC Conference - Activity Details – Award Finalist/Winner|access-date= 27 July 2015}}</ref> In 2010, Szalay began developing the Data-Scope, a 6.5PB system with 500Gbytes/s sequential throughput, utilizing a uniquely balanced system built out of hard disks, SSDs and GPUs, for maximal data flow across the system.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://releases.jhu.edu/2010/11/01/new-jhu-computer-to-enable-data-analysis-not-possible-today/|title= New JHU Computer To Enable Data Analysis Not Possible Today|last1=De Nike |first1= Lisa|date= 1 November 2010 |publisher= Johns Hopkins University|access-date= 28 July 2015 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url= https://nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=1040114 |title= MRI: Development of Data-Scope - A Multi-Petabyte Generic Data Analysis Environment for Science|access-date= 28 July 2015}}</ref> The Data-Scope went online in 2013 and read “data 30 times faster than GrayWulf, making it the fastest data-processing system at any university in the world.”<ref name="Johns Hopkins University"/>

Szalay has more recently branched out in other scientific areas focusing on data-intensive computing.<ref>{{cite journal|last1= Szalay|first1= Alexander|last2= Gray|first2= Jim|date= 23 March 2006|title= 2020 Computing: Science in an exponential world|journal= [[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|publisher= Macmillan Publishers Limited|volume= 440|issue= 7083|pages =413–414|doi= 10.1038/440413a|bibcode = 2006Natur.440..413S|pmid=16554783|hdl= 1885/46877|s2cid= 4360446|hdl-access= free}}</ref> In collaboration with [[Randal Burns]], [[Charles Meneveau]], and [http://www.ams.jhu.edu/~eyink/ Greg Eyink], he has built the 350TB turbulence database (JHTDB) providing immersive access to a large [[computational fluid dynamics]] simulation, where users can launch [[Virtual sensing|virtual sensors]] into the simulation that report back their [[velocity]]. A landmark paper using these resources appeared in ''Nature''.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Eyink|first1=Gregory|last2=Vishniac|first2=Ethan| last3=Lalescu|first3=Christian|last4=Aluie|first4=Hussein|last5=Kanov|first5=Kalin|last6=Burger|first6=Kai|last7=Burns|first7=Randal|last8=Meneveau|first8=Charles|last9=Szalay|first9=Alexander|date= 23 May 2013|title= Flux-freezing breakdown in high-conductivity magnetohydrodynamic turbulence |journal= [[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|publisher= Macmillan Publishers Limited|volume= 497|issue=7450|pages =466–469|doi= 10.1038/nature12128|bibcode = 2013Natur.497..466E |pmid=23698445|s2cid=205233857}}</ref>

With Andreas Terzis and Katalin Szlavecz, he has built an end-to-end wireless sensor system for [[in-situ]] monitoring of environmental parameters, including [[Carbon dioxide|{{CO2}}]], and measuring the impact of the soil on the [[global carbon cycle]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1= Terzis|first1= Andreas|last2= Szlavecz |first2= Katalin |last3=Szalay|first3=Alexander|date= 2010|title= Wireless sensor networks for soil science |url= http://www.inderscienceonline.com/doi/abs/10.1504/IJSNet.2010.03185 |journal= International Journal of Sensor Networks|publisher= Inderscience Enterprises Ltd.|volume= 7|issue= 1/2|pages =53–70|doi= 10.1504/IJSNet.2010.03185 |access-date=27 July 2015|doi-broken-date= 11 July 2025}}</ref> With sensors around [[Baltimore]], Brazil, [[Ecuador]] and the [[Atacama Desert]] in [[Chile]], the system has more than 200,000 sensor days of data and several hundred million [[data points]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1= Terzis|first1= Andreas|last2= Szlavecz |first2= Katalin |last3=Szalay|first3=Alexander|last4=Gupchap|first4=Jayant|date= December 2008|title= Deploying Advanced Wireless Sensor Networks for Ecological Monitoring|url= http://research.microsoft.com/apps/video/default.aspx?id=137339&r=1|journal= Microsoft eScience Workshop|publisher= Microsoft Research|access-date=27 July 2015}}</ref>

Szalay has also become heavily involved in applying modern data-intensive computational techniques to [[genomics]], in collaboration with [[Steven Salzberg]], Ben Langmead, Sarah Wheelan, and Richard Wilton. The collaboration has built a new alignment system for [[genomics]], which is substantially faster than any other system today.<ref>{{cite journal|last1= Wilton|first1= Richard|last2= Wheelan |first2= Sarah |last3=Szalay|first3=Alexander|last4=Salzberg|first4=Steven|last5=Langmead|first5=Ben|last6=Buvavari|first6=Tamas|date= 3 March 2015|title= Arioc: high-throughput read alignment with GPU-accelerated exploration of the seed-and-extend search space|journal= PeerJ Comput. Sci. |publisher= PeerJ |volume= 3 |pages= e808 |doi= 10.7717/peerj.808 |pmid= 25780763|pmc= 4358639|doi-access= free}}</ref>

== Publications ==
He has written over 575 papers in various scientific journals, covering areas from [[theoretical cosmology]] to [[observational astronomy]], [[spatial statistics]] and [[computer science]], and more recently [[turbulence]], [[environmental science]] and [[genomics]]. Szalay has more than 63,805 citations in Google Scholar and an h-index of 96.<ref name="Author: A.S. Szalay">Google Scholar [https://scholar.google.co.uk/citations?user=rUiWchkAAAAJ&hl=en&oi=sra "Author: A.S. Szalay"], ''[[Google Scholar]]'', 27 July 2015. Retrieved on 27 July 2015.</ref>

He was among the top 1% most cited in the world for subject field and year of publication in the 2001 and 2014 [[Thomson Reuters]] Highly Cited Researchers reports.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://highlycited.com/#szalay|title= Highly Cited Researchers 2014, Highly Cited Researchers 2001|access-date= 28 July 2015}}</ref>
